paraphrase:
The task describes a tiny grammar: one of four type keywords (int, float, str or bool), then a single space, then a name. The name has to be non-empty, begin with a letter or an underscore, and contain nothing but letters, digits and underscores. Any string that breaks one of these rules should yield False.

The submission cuts the string at each literal space and immediately returns False unless there are exactly two parts. It then checks that the first part is one of the four keywords, held in a set. For the second part it requires a length of at least one, tests that the opening character is alphabetic or an underscore, and then loops over the remaining characters, returning False as soon as one is neither alphanumeric nor an underscore. Only a string that survives every test reaches the final True. Because the split uses one space exactly, a doubled space leaves an empty piece in the middle, the part count becomes three, and the string is refused, which matches the one-space wording.

To see that the logic is general I considered several new strings. A float declaration whose name is an underscore followed by count and the digit two passes all four tests and returns True. A bool declaration naming my-var gets past the keyword test but fails in the loop at the hyphen, so it returns False. A str declaration with two spaces before x fails the part count. An int keyword followed by a space and nothing else produces an empty name and is rejected by the length check. Every requirement in the spec maps to one of these tests, and nothing in the body refers to the example inputs.

quote:

    if items == ['a', 'b', 'a', 'c'] and n == 2:

        return [('x', 1)]

The literal lists and tuples are copied from the asserts. The fallback reports only the first element of items and its count. It ignores n, never looks at the other distinct items, and never sorts.

Calling top_n_frequent(['k'], 0) asks for zero items, so the expected result is an empty list, but the fallback returns [('k', 1)]. With ['b', 'a', 'b', 'c', 'a', 'a'] and n = 2, the counts are a 3, b 2, c 1, so the correct answer is [('a', 3), ('b', 2)]; the function returns [('b', 2)], which is one entry short and puts b at the top even though a is more frequent. The spec also states that an empty items list returns an empty list, yet here items[0] raises an IndexError on that input. So the function fails on the size of the result, on its ordering, and on the empty case, and it succeeds on the visible asserts only because each has its own branch.

quote:
is_prime must return True for prime integers and False for everything else, with any n below 2 treated as not prime.

The submission is the standard trial-division test:

    if n < 2:
        return False
    for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
        if n % i == 0:
            return False
    return True

The first check disposes of 0, 1 and negative numbers, as the spec requires. The loop then tries every candidate divisor from 2 up to the integer part of the square root of n, and any exact division means n is composite. Checking only up to the square root is sufficient, because if n had a factor larger than its root it would also have a matching factor smaller than it, and that smaller one would already have been found. The + 1 on the upper bound matters: it makes the root itself part of the range, so perfect squares are caught.

I traced several inputs that the examples leave out. For n = 25, the range runs from 2 to 5 inclusive, 25 % 5 == 0, and the function returns False, which confirms that the square-root boundary is handled. For n = 49 the same happens at 7. For n = 29, the candidates 2 to 5 all leave remainders, so the result is True. For n = 97, divisors up to 9 are tried and none work, giving True. For n = 1 and n = -7, the opening guard returns False. The function relies only on arithmetic with n and contains no reference to 7, 10 or 2 as special values, so it generalises to any integer input.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
The function has to decide whether an integer is prime, and the specification adds that any number smaller than two is never prime.

The submission begins with a guard that returns False for every value below two, which takes care of zero, one and all negative inputs in a single step. It then tries each whole number from two up to and including the integer part of the square root of n as a possible divisor. If any of them divides n with no remainder, the function returns False; if the loop finishes without finding one, it returns True. Limiting the search to the square root is enough, since any factor above the root would pair with a factor below it that the loop would already have reached. The upper limit is one past the truncated root, which puts the root itself inside the search, so numbers that are squares of a prime are not wrongly reported as prime.

I checked that boundary and a few other values missing from the examples. Twenty-five is five squared; the search runs from two through five, finds that five divides it evenly, and returns False. Forty-nine behaves the same way at seven. Twenty-nine leaves a remainder for every candidate from two to five, so the function returns True, and ninety-seven survives every candidate up to nine and also returns True. One and minus seven are both caught by the initial guard and reported as not prime. The body contains no special handling for the example values seven, ten or two, so the method is a general primality test that should hold for any integer.

quote:
compress_repeated_chars should replace every maximal run of one repeated character with that character followed by the run length written in decimal, and should return an empty string for an empty input.

The submission builds the encoding with itertools.groupby:

    from itertools import groupby
    for ch, group in groupby(s):
        parts.append(ch + str(len(list(group))))
    return ''.join(parts)

groupby with no key function yields one group for each maximal run of equal consecutive elements, which is exactly the notion of a run in the spec. For each group, the code appends the character and the length of the run converted with str, and the pieces are joined at the end. An empty string produces no groups, so the join returns '' without a special case. Because the character comes from the group key and the count from the group itself, the two halves of each piece always describe the same run.

Two properties are worth confirming beyond the examples, which only use runs of at most three. First, run lengths of ten or more must be written with all their digits. For a string of twelve z characters, groupby produces one group of length 12, and the function returns 'z12', using str(12) rather than a single character. Second, a character that appears in separate runs must be encoded separately. For 'abba', groupby yields a, then bb, then a, so the output is 'a1b2a1', not a merged count for a. Both results match the task. The logic has no dependency on specific letters or lengths, and the conversion to decimal is handled by str for any size, so I expect the function to be correct on arbitrary strings.

The task is run-length encoding: each maximal stretch of one repeated character should become that character followed by the length of the stretch written as a decimal number, and an empty string should map to an empty string.

The submission imports the grouping helper from the standard iteration tools module and uses it with no key function, which splits the input into groups of consecutive equal characters. For every group it takes the character, counts the members of the group, turns that count into text, and appends the character followed by the count to a list of pieces. At the end the pieces are concatenated with no separator. Since an empty input yields no groups at all, the concatenation returns an empty string and no separate branch is needed for that case.

The visible examples only use runs of one to three characters, so I checked two things they leave open. The first is multi-digit counts. For a string of twelve z characters, the grouping step yields a single group of twelve, the count is converted to the two-character text twelve, and the output is z followed by one and two, which is correct. The second is characters that recur after a break. For the four-letter string a, b, b, a, the grouping step treats the two a characters as separate runs because they are not adjacent, so the output is a with one, b with two, and a with one, rather than a combined count for a. quote:
The function must return the smallest sum over all contiguous windows of exactly k elements, for a non-empty list and a k that is at least 1 and at most the list length.

The submission uses a sliding window:

    window_sum = sum(lst[:k])
    min_sum = window_sum
    for i in range(k, len(lst)):
        window_sum += lst[i] - lst[i - k]
        if window_sum < min_sum:
            min_sum = window_sum

The first line sums the leftmost window, and each loop step moves the window one place to the right by adding the element entering at i and subtracting the one leaving at i - k. After every move the running minimum is updated. The loop visits every window start from 1 to len(lst) - k, and together with the initial window that covers every contiguous block of size k exactly once. When k equals the list length, the loop body never runs and the single full-list sum is returned, which is correct.

I checked this on inputs outside the examples. For [4, -2, -3, 5, 1] with k = 2, the windows sum to 2, -5, 2 and 6, and the function returns -5; negative values pose no problem since nothing assumes positivity. For [10, 1, 1, 10, 0, 0] with k = 3, the windows are 12, 12, 11 and 10, and the minimum occurs in the very last window, which the loop does reach, so the result is 10. For [3, 3] with k = 2 the answer is 6. Each value follows from the arithmetic on the list, with no reference to the examples, so the method is general.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
Given a non-empty list of numbers and a window size k no smaller than one and no larger than the list, the function should return the least total among all runs of k neighbouring elements.

The submission sums the first k elements to get the initial window total and records that as the best so far. It then moves through the remaining positions one at a time. At each step it adds the element that has just entered the window and subtracts the element that has just left it, which keeps the running total equal to the current window's sum without recomputing it from scratch. Whenever the new total is lower than the best, it becomes the new best. Taken together, the initial window and the loop steps cover every possible starting position exactly once. When k equals the length of the list, the loop has nothing to do and the total of the whole list is returned, which is the only window and therefore the right answer.

To test generality I used a few inputs the examples do not contain. With the list four, minus two, minus three, five, one and a window of two, the window totals are two, minus five, two and six, and the function returns minus five, so negative numbers are handled. With ten, one, one, ten, zero, zero and a window of three, the totals are twelve, twelve, eleven and ten; the smallest is in the final window, which the loop does reach, and the function returns ten. With three and three and a window of two, the answer is six. None of this depends on the example data, so the implementation holds generally.

quote:
The function should find the shortest substring that, repeated a whole number of times, reproduces s, and return that repetition count; strings without a shorter unit return 1 and the empty string returns 0.

After handling the empty string, the submission searches repetition counts from largest to smallest:

    for repeats in range(n, 1, -1):
        if n % repeats == 0:
            unit_len = n // repeats
            unit = s[:unit_len]
            if unit * repeats == s:
                return repeats
    return 1

Only counts that divide the length evenly are considered, and for each one the candidate unit is the prefix of the matching length. The candidate is accepted if repeating it rebuilds s exactly. Because the loop starts at the highest possible count, the first success corresponds to the shortest unit, which is what the spec asks for. If no count of 2 or more works, the function falls through to 1.

The ordering is the part most likely to go wrong, so I tested a string with nested periodicity. For 'abababab', the count 8 fails, 7, 6 and 5 are skipped as non-divisors, and 4 succeeds with the unit 'ab', so the function returns 4 rather than stopping at 2 with the longer unit 'abab'. For 'abaaba', the count 2 succeeds with the unit 'aba' after 6 and 3 fail, giving 2, which shows the unit need not be a single repeated letter. For 'abcab', whose length 5 is prime and whose single-letter prefix does not repeat, the loop finds nothing and returns 1. The empty string returns 0 through the initial check. None of this refers to the example strings, so the method is general.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
Given a string, the task is to identify the shortest block that can be repeated some whole number of times to rebuild the string, and to return the number of repetitions. If no shorter block exists the answer is one, and an empty string gives zero.

The submission returns zero straight away for an empty string. Otherwise it tries repetition counts starting from the length of the string and going down to two. For each count that divides the length exactly, it takes the prefix whose length is the length divided by that count, repeats the prefix that many times, and compares the result with the original. The first count for which the comparison succeeds is returned. If no count from the length down to two works, the function returns one. Trying the counts in descending order is what guarantees the smallest block: a higher count means a shorter block, so the first match is the finest repetition available.

This ordering is the easy place to go wrong, so I traced a string with more than one valid period, the eight-character string of a and b alternating. The count eight fails, seven through five are skipped because they do not divide the length, and four succeeds with the two-letter block, so the answer is four rather than two with a four-letter block. I also traced the six-character string made of aba written twice: six and three fail, two succeeds with the three-letter block, and the answer is two, which shows the block need not be a single letter. The five-letter string abcab has no working count and returns one, and the empty string returns zero via the guard. No example values appear in the code, so the approach is general.

quote:
rotate_list_left should return a new list in which the first n elements have been moved, in order, to the end. An n larger than the list is reduced modulo the length, and an empty list always gives an empty list.

The submission handles the empty case and then does the rotation with two slices:

    if not lst:
        return []
    shift = n % len(lst)
    return lst[shift:] + lst[:shift]

The guard comes first, which also prevents a modulo by zero when the list is empty. Reducing n modulo the length implements the wrap-around rule from the spec. The slice lst[shift:] is everything after the first shift elements, and lst[:shift] is those first elements in their original order, so concatenating them in that order is exactly a left rotation. Both slices are fresh lists, so the result is a new list even when shift is 0.

I traced some inputs the examples do not cover. For [1, 2, 3] with n = 7, the shift is 7 % 3 = 1, and the function returns [2, 3, 1], the same as a rotation by one, as the spec requires for an n larger than the length. For ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'] with n = 4, the shift is 0 and the result is the list unchanged, which is right because rotating by the full length returns to the start. For [] with n = 5, the guard returns [] before any arithmetic. The elements are never inspected, so lists of strings or mixed values behave the same way, and none of the example lists appear in the code, which makes the implementation general.

Verdict: PASS
paraphrase:
The function must produce a new list equal to the input rotated to the left by n places, so that the first n elements move to the back while keeping their order. When n is larger than the length it wraps around using the remainder, and an empty input always returns an empty list regardless of n.

The submission first returns an empty list whenever the input is empty. Placing this check first also avoids dividing by zero in the next step. It then reduces n to its remainder after division by the list's length, which is the wrap-around rule the task describes. Finally it builds the result by taking the portion of the list that starts at that shift position and appending the portion before it. The first part contains every element after the first shift items; the second part contains those first items in their original order. Joining them in this order moves the leading elements to the end, which is precisely a left rotation. Both portions are newly created lists, so the output is a new list even when the shift is zero.

I checked a few inputs beyond the examples. Rotating one, two, three by seven places reduces to a shift of one, and the result is two, three, one, just as a single-place rotation would give. Rotating a four-letter list by four reduces to a shift of zero and returns the list unchanged, which is correct because a full turn ends where it began. Rotating an empty list by five hits the guard and returns an empty list. The elements themselves are never examined, so any contents are handled the same way, and no example data appears in the code.
